Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ and $Y:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(T,\mathcal T)$ be measurable random elements. A **conditional law of X given Y** is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that $\omega\mapsto K(Y(\omega),\cdot)$ is a regular conditional distribution of X given $\sigma(Y)$ in [[def-regular-conditional-distribution]]. Thus for every $A\in\mathcal S$ and $H\in\sigma(Y)$,
$$\int_H K(Y(\omega),A)\,dP=P(H\cap\{X\in A\}).$$

Composition with Y makes each evaluation $\sigma(Y)$-measurable, and every section remains a probability by [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. The notation $P(X\in A\mid Y=y)=K(y,A)$ refers to a chosen kernel; it is not a ratio involving the possibly zero probability $P(Y=y)$.

Write $P_Y(B)=P(Y^{-1}(B))$ for the law in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]. If a specified countable family $\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal S$ determines probability measures, two conditional laws K,L agree as measures outside a single $\mathcal T$-measurable $P_Y$-null set. Indeed for each $A\in\mathcal C$ the measurable discrepancy $D_A=\{y:K(y,A)\ne L(y,A)\}$ has null inverse image under Y by [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]]. Hence $P_Y(D_A)=0$ by the law definition; the countable union $D$ is null by [[thm-finite-and-countable-subadditivity-of-measures]], and off D the determining property gives equality of measures. This uses a supplied determining family and makes no AC assertion about obtaining one.

Values on a measurable $P_Y$-null subset may be replaced by a specified fixed probability on E without changing these identities. The inverse image of that subset is measurable null, and all event evaluations are bounded, so the modified event integrals agree. Empty-event evaluations remain zero and whole-target evaluations remain one. Existence on standard-Borel spaces is proved separately; the definition alone does not assert a conditional kernel exists.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

A family $(\mathcal F_i)_{i\in I}$ of sub-sigma-algebras of $\mathcal F$ is
**independent** when it is independent as a family of event classes in the
sense of [[def-independent-families-of-event-classes]].

A family $(A_i)_{i\in I}$ of events is **independent** when the singleton event
classes $\bigl(\{A_i\}\bigr)_{i\in I}$ are independent. Equivalently, for every
finite choice of distinct indices $i_0,\dots,i_{n-1}$,

$$\mathbb P\left(\bigcap_{k<n}A_{i_k}\right)=\prod_{k<n}\mathbb P(A_{i_k}).$$

For two events this reduces to the familiar identity
$\mathbb P(A\cap B)=\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)$.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(T,\Tau)$ be a measurable random element and $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra. A **regular conditional distribution of X given $\mathcal G$** is a probability kernel $K:(\Omega,\mathcal G)\to(T,\Tau)$ satisfying
$$\int_H K(\omega,A)\,P(d\omega)=P(H\cap\{X\in A\})\qquad(H\in\mathcal G,\ A\in\Tau).$$

“Probability kernel” has the pointwise meaning of [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]: every $K(\omega,\cdot)$ is a probability measure, and every evaluation is $\mathcal G$-measurable. Its evaluations lie in $[0,1]$ and are integrable. Thus the testing identity says exactly that $K(\cdot,A)$ is a conditional-expectation version of $1_{\{X\in A\}}$ in [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. Conversely, a probability kernel with these version identities satisfies the displayed definition.

The kernel requirement holds at every sample point. Separate eventwise choices of conditional-expectation versions do not imply it and do not by themselves provide one exceptional set valid for all A. When A is empty the testing identity is zero on both sides, and when A=T it is P(H) on both sides. This defines a property of a supplied kernel and makes no existence or AC assertion.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

derivations.claim: Write $\mu=\mathcal L(Z)$. For every $h$, the product $\Lambda(h,\cdot)=\kappa(h,\cdot)\otimes\mu$ is a probability measure by [F2] and [F3]. For each $D\in\mathcal E\otimes\mathcal W$, the section $x\mapsto\mu(D_x)$ is measurable by [F4] applied to the constant probability kernel $\mu$ and the indicator of $D$. The iterated-section formula in [F3] gives $\Lambda(h,D)=\int_E\mu(D_x)\,\kappa(h,dx)$, which is measurable in $h$ by [F4] applied to $\kappa$. Thus $\Lambda$ is a probability kernel.

Fix $C\in\sigma(Y)$ and a measurable rectangle $A\times B$. The conditional-law identity [F1], followed by independence [F6]–[F7], gives $\int_C\Lambda(Y,A\times B)\,d\mathbb P=\mu(B)\int_C\kappa(Y,A)\,d\mathbb P=\mu(B)\mathbb P(C\cap\{X\in A\})=\mathbb P(C\cap\{X\in A,Z\in B\})$. For this fixed $C$, both sides define finite measures on $\mathcal E\otimes\mathcal W$. They agree on the rectangle pi-system, which generates that sigma-algebra by [F5]; [F9] extends the equality to every measurable target set. Therefore $\Lambda(Y,\cdot)$ is a regular conditional distribution of $(X,Z)$ given $\sigma(Y)$ by [F8].

For measurable $\Phi$, every section of $\Lambda^\Phi$ is the pushforward of the probability $\Lambda(h,\cdot)$, and its evaluations are measurable because $\Phi^{-1}(C)$ is measurable and $\Lambda$ is a probability kernel. Applying the conditional identity from step 1.2 to $\Phi^{-1}(C)$ proves that $\Lambda^\Phi(Y,\cdot)$ is a regular conditional distribution of $\Phi(X,Z)$ given $\sigma(Y)$. Hence it is the required conditional law.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $m\ge1$ be finite, let $d_j\ge1$, and let
$Z_j$ for $1\le j\le m$ be mutually independent random elements of
$\mathbb R^{d_j}$. Suppose $Z_j\sim N_{d_j}(a_j,\Sigma_j)$, where each
$\Sigma_j$ is symmetric positive semidefinite. Put
$D=\sum_{j=1}^m d_j$, $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$,
$a=(a_1,\ldots,a_m)$, and
$\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\Sigma_1,\ldots,\Sigma_m)$. Then
$$Z\sim N_D(a,\Sigma).$$
No covariance block needs to be invertible.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be non-negative. Then there exists a unique non-negative operator
$R:V\to V$ such that

$$R^2=T.$$

Assume AC. Let $X\in\mathbb R^d$ and $Y\in\mathbb R^m$, with $d,m\ge1$, be
jointly multivariate normal with mean $(a,b)$ and positive-semidefinite block
covariance
$$\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}A&C\\C^T&B\end{pmatrix},$$
where $B$ is positive definite. Then
$$S=A-CB^{-1}C^T$$
is positive semidefinite, and for every $y\in\mathbb R^m$ the probability law
$$K(y,\cdot)=N_d\!\left(a+CB^{-1}(y-b),S\right)$$
is defined. The map $K$ is a probability kernel and is a conditional law of
$X$ given $Y$: for all Borel $E\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ and
$F\subseteq\mathbb R^m$,
$$\mathbb P(X\in E,Y\in F)=\int_F K(y,E)\,\mathbb P_Y(dy).$$
The covariance $A$ and the conditional covariance $S$ may be singular.
Positive definiteness of $B$ is required; no pseudoinverse formula for
singular $B$ is asserted.

derivations.claim: By [F2], the stack $(U,q,r)$ is jointly Gaussian with mean $(m,0,0)$ and covariance $\operatorname{diag}(P,Q,R)$. For any $a\in\mathbb R^n$ and $b\in\mathbb R^p$, the scalar $a^TX+b^TY$ is a linear projection of this stack, so it is normal by [F1]; thus $(X,Y)$ is jointly Gaussian. Since $q$ is independent of $U$ and centered, $\operatorname{Cov}(X)=F\operatorname{Cov}(U)F^T+\operatorname{Cov}(q)=FPF^T+Q=P^-$. Since $Y=HX+r$ and $r$ is independent of $X$ and centered, $\mathbb E X=Fm$, $\mathbb E Y=HFm$, $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=P^-H^T$, and $\operatorname{Cov}(Y)=HP^-H^T+R=S$. Hence the block covariance is the one displayed in the Statement and is positive semidefinite as a covariance matrix. Also $P^-\succeq0$, since $u^TP^-u=(F^Tu)^TP(F^Tu)+u^TQu\ge0$ for every $u$.

Apply [F4] with $A=P^-$, $C=P^-H^T$, and $B=S$. The observed block is positive definite by hypothesis, and the joint block is positive semidefinite by step 1.1. The conditional mean is $Fm+P^-H^TS^{-1}(y-HFm)=Fm+K(y-HFm)$. Its covariance is $P^--P^-H^TS^{-1}HP^-=P^--KSK^T$, and [F4] makes it positive semidefinite and gives a conditional-law version for every $y$.

Since $S=HP^-H^T+R$ and $K=P^-H^TS^{-1}$, symmetry of $P^-$ and $S$ gives $KHP^-=P^-H^TK^T=KSK^T$. Expanding the Joseph expression yields $P^- -KHP^- -P^-H^TK^T+K(HP^-H^T+R)K^T=P^--KSK^T$. It is positive semidefinite because [F4] gives that covariance this property; independently, the Joseph expression is a sum of positive-semidefinite matrices. This proves the identity without inverting $P$, $Q$, or $R$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$. Let
the state dimension at time
$t$ be a positive integer $d_t$ for $0\le t\le T$, and the observation
dimension at time $t$ be a positive integer $p_t$ for $1\le t\le T$.
Choose deterministic matrices
$F_t\in\mathbb R^{d_t\times d_{t-1}}$ and
$H_t\in\mathbb R^{p_t\times d_t}$, a mean $m_0\in\mathbb R^{d_0}$, and
symmetric positive-semidefinite matrices, meaning $v^TPv\ge0$ for every
real vector $v$ of matching dimension,
$P_0\in\mathbb R^{d_0\times d_0}$,
$Q_t\in\mathbb R^{d_t\times d_t}$, and
$R_t\in\mathbb R^{p_t\times p_t}$. A **linear-Gaussian state-space model
with independent noises** is the general finite-horizon kernel model
([[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]) with initial law
$\mu_0=N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$ and transition and observation kernels
$$K_t(x,\cdot)=N_{d_t}(F_t x,Q_t),\qquad G_t(x,\cdot)=N_{p_t}(H_t x,R_t).$$
All Gaussian laws use the convention of
[[def-multivariate-normal-law]], which allows singular covariance matrices.

Its independent-noise representation consists of random vectors
$x_0,q_1,r_1,\ldots,q_T,r_T$ on a common probability space, with
$x_0\sim N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$, $q_t\sim N_{d_t}(0,Q_t)$,
$r_t\sim N_{p_t}(0,R_t)$, all mutually independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-random-elements]] (their generated sigma-algebras are
independent), and equations
$$x_t=F_t x_{t-1}+q_t,\qquad y_t=H_t x_t+r_t\qquad(1\le t\le T).$$
The local path-law theorem proves that every allowed parameter tuple has
such a finite representation, that its induced kernels are the displayed
$K_t,G_t$, and that its path law is the general kernel-product law.

This definition imposes the stated noise law and independence assumptions;
it does not establish their empirical adequacy. It supplies no filtering
algorithm, posterior recursion, or convergence claim. Any separate formula
that inverts an observed innovation covariance must assume that covariance is
positive definite at the point of inversion.

Assume AC and fix a finite-horizon model of
[[def-linear-gaussian-state-space-model-with-independent-noises]]. There is a
probability space carrying mutually independent Gaussian vectors
$x_0,q_1,r_1,\ldots,q_T,r_T$ with the stated laws. The recursions
$x_t=F_t x_{t-1}+q_t$ and $y_t=H_t x_t+r_t$ induce the general kernel-product
law of [[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. In the interleaved order
$Z_T=(x_0,x_1,y_1,\ldots,x_T,y_T)$, there is a deterministic matrix $M_T$
such that
$$Z_T=M_T W_T,\qquad W_T=(x_0,q_1,r_1,\ldots,q_T,r_T),$$
and
$$Z_T\sim N\!\left(M_T a_T,\ M_T\Sigma_T M_T^T\right),\qquad a_T=(m_0,0,\ldots,0),\quad \Sigma_T=\operatorname{diag}(P_0,Q_1,R_1,\ldots,Q_T,R_T).$$
The covariance may be singular.

Assume AC and fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$ with a state-space model by
probability kernels as in
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. If $T=0$, put $\Omega_T=E_0$;
otherwise put $\Omega_T=E_0\times E_1\times F_1\times\cdots\times E_T\times
F_T$. Let $\mathcal Z_T$ be the corresponding finite-product sigma-algebra
and write $(\Omega_T,\mathcal Z_T,P_T)$ for its finite-horizon probability
space. The law $P_T$ is the unique law supplied by
[[thm-finite-horizon-state-space-kernel-law-exists-uniquely]]. Let $X_t$ and
$Y_t$ be the coordinate random elements taking values in $E_t$ and $F_t$. For
$t\ge1$, write $Y_{1:t}:=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_t)$ and
$\mathsf F_{1:t}:=F_1\times\cdots\times F_t$ with its finite-product
sigma-algebra; let $\mathsf F_{1:0}$ be a singleton and $Y_{1:0}$ its constant
map. The factors are standard Borel, meaning measurably isomorphic to Polish
spaces ([[def-standard-borel-space]]), and their finite products are standard
Borel ([[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]]).

The **initial filtering kernel** $\pi_0:\mathsf F_{1:0}\to E_0$ assigns
$\mu_0$ to the unique empty history; it is the conditional law of $X_0$ given
the trivial history. For $1\le t\le T$, a **filtering kernel at time $t$** is
a probability kernel $\pi_t:\mathsf F_{1:t}\to E_t$ such that
$\omega\mapsto\pi_t(Y_{1:t}(\omega),\cdot)$ is a regular conditional
distribution of $X_t$ given $\sigma(Y_{1:t})$. For $1\le t\le T$, a
**predictive kernel at time $t$** is a probability kernel
$\pi_{t|t-1}:\mathsf F_{1:t-1}\to E_t$ whose composition with $Y_{1:t-1}$
is a regular conditional distribution of $X_t$ given
$\sigma(Y_{1:t-1})$. A **finite-horizon smoothing kernel** is a probability
kernel $\psi_T:\mathsf F_{1:T}\to E_0\times\cdots\times E_T$ whose
composition with $Y_{1:T}$ is a regular conditional distribution of the full
state path $(X_0,\ldots,X_T)$ given $\sigma(Y_{1:T})$. Here a regular
conditional distribution is an everywhere probability kernel satisfying the
conditional event identities in
[[def-regular-conditional-distribution]], and a conditional law given a
random element is its data-indexed kernel form in
[[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]].

These kernels are versions: their values can be changed on a measurable set
of observation histories of probability zero without changing the conditional
identities. No density is assumed in these definitions. The state-space model
here is one fixed law. A parametric statistical model is instead a map
$\theta\mapsto P_\theta$ from a parameter set to probability laws; its
measurability is not asserted without a parameter sigma-algebra
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]).

Assume AC and a finite-horizon state-space model by standard-Borel state and
observation spaces, an initial probability measure, and transition and
observation probability kernels, as in
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. Let $P_T$ be its finite-horizon
path law. The initial filtering kernel is $\pi_0=\mu_0$ on the singleton
empty-history space. For each $1\le t\le T$, data-indexed filtering and
predictive kernels from [[def-state-space-filtering-laws]] exist. A
data-indexed finite-horizon smoothing kernel for the full state path also
exists, including when $T=0$. The claim is existence of conditional versions
only; it asserts no density, filtering recursion, uniqueness on null
observation histories, or numerical approximation.

Let $X,Y,Z$ be random elements with values in measurable spaces
$(E,\mathcal E)$, $(H,\mathcal H)$, and $(W,\mathcal W)$. Suppose $Z$ is
independent of the random element $(X,Y)$, and let
$\kappa:H\to E$ be a supplied conditional law of $X$ given $Y$. For each
$h\in H$, form the product probability
$\Lambda(h,\cdot)=\kappa(h,\cdot)\otimes\mathcal L(Z)$ on
$\mathcal E\otimes\mathcal W$. Then $\Lambda$ is a conditional law of
$(X,Z)$ given $Y$. If $\Phi:E\times W\to V$ is measurable into a measurable
space $(V,\mathcal V)$, then
$$\Lambda^\Phi(h,C):=\Lambda(h,\Phi^{-1}(C))$$
is a conditional law of $\Phi(X,Z)$ given $Y$.

Assume AC, and let $d,n,p$ be positive integers. Let $U\in\mathbb R^d$,
$q\in\mathbb R^n$, and $r\in\mathbb R^p$ be mutually independent Gaussian vectors with
$$U\sim N_d(m,P),\qquad q\sim N_n(0,Q),\qquad r\sim N_p(0,R),$$
where $P,Q,R$ are symmetric positive semidefinite. Let
$F\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$ and $H\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}$, and set
$$X=FU+q,\qquad Y=HX+r,\qquad P^-:=FPF^T+Q,\qquad S:=HP^-H^T+R.$$
If $S$ is positive definite, put $K:=P^-H^TS^{-1}$. Then $(X,Y)$ is jointly
Gaussian with mean $(Fm,HFm)$ and covariance
$$\begin{pmatrix}P^-&P^-H^T\\HP^-&S\end{pmatrix},$$
and for every $y\in\mathbb R^p$ an everywhere-defined conditional law is
$$\mathcal L(X\mid Y=y)=N_n\!\left(Fm+K(y-HFm),\,P^--KSK^T\right).$$
The conditional covariance is positive semidefinite even if $P$, $Q$, or
$R$ is singular. It also equals the Joseph expression
$$(I-KH)P^-(I-KH)^T+KRK^T.$$
No inverse of a state, process-noise, or measurement-noise covariance is
used.

Assume AC. Let $X\in\mathbb R^d$ and $Y\in\mathbb R^m$, with $d,m\ge1$, be
jointly multivariate normal with mean $(a,b)$ and positive-semidefinite block
covariance
$$\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}A&C\\C^T&B\end{pmatrix},$$
where $B$ is positive definite. Then
$$S=A-CB^{-1}C^T$$
is positive semidefinite, and for every $y\in\mathbb R^m$ the probability law
$$K(y,\cdot)=N_d\!\left(a+CB^{-1}(y-b),S\right)$$
is defined. The map $K$ is a probability kernel and is a conditional law of
$X$ given $Y$: for all Borel $E\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ and
$F\subseteq\mathbb R^m$,
$$\mathbb P(X\in E,Y\in F)=\int_F K(y,E)\,\mathbb P_Y(dy).$$
The covariance $A$ and the conditional covariance $S$ may be singular.
Positive definiteness of $B$ is required; no pseudoinverse formula for
singular $B$ is asserted.

Let $n\ge 1$ and let $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$, with the real case obtained by
restricting scalars to $\mathbb R$. Then the following are equivalent:

1. $A$ has a Cholesky factorisation $A=LL^*$ with $L$ lower triangular and
   positive real diagonal.
2. $A$ is Hermitian positive definite.

When these conditions hold, the factor $L$ is unique.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be non-negative. Then there exists a unique non-negative operator
$R:V\to V$ such that

$$R^2=T.$$

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$. Let
the state dimension at time
$t$ be a positive integer $d_t$ for $0\le t\le T$, and the observation
dimension at time $t$ be a positive integer $p_t$ for $1\le t\le T$.
Choose deterministic matrices
$F_t\in\mathbb R^{d_t\times d_{t-1}}$ and
$H_t\in\mathbb R^{p_t\times d_t}$, a mean $m_0\in\mathbb R^{d_0}$, and
symmetric positive-semidefinite matrices, meaning $v^TPv\ge0$ for every
real vector $v$ of matching dimension,
$P_0\in\mathbb R^{d_0\times d_0}$,
$Q_t\in\mathbb R^{d_t\times d_t}$, and
$R_t\in\mathbb R^{p_t\times p_t}$. A **linear-Gaussian state-space model
with independent noises** is the general finite-horizon kernel model
([[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]) with initial law
$\mu_0=N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$ and transition and observation kernels
$$K_t(x,\cdot)=N_{d_t}(F_t x,Q_t),\qquad G_t(x,\cdot)=N_{p_t}(H_t x,R_t).$$
All Gaussian laws use the convention of
[[def-multivariate-normal-law]], which allows singular covariance matrices.

Its independent-noise representation consists of random vectors
$x_0,q_1,r_1,\ldots,q_T,r_T$ on a common probability space, with
$x_0\sim N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$, $q_t\sim N_{d_t}(0,Q_t)$,
$r_t\sim N_{p_t}(0,R_t)$, all mutually independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-random-elements]] (their generated sigma-algebras are
independent), and equations
$$x_t=F_t x_{t-1}+q_t,\qquad y_t=H_t x_t+r_t\qquad(1\le t\le T).$$
The local path-law theorem proves that every allowed parameter tuple has
such a finite representation, that its induced kernels are the displayed
$K_t,G_t$, and that its path law is the general kernel-product law.

This definition imposes the stated noise law and independence assumptions;
it does not establish their empirical adequacy. It supplies no filtering
algorithm, posterior recursion, or convergence claim. Any separate formula
that inverts an observed innovation covariance must assume that covariance is
positive definite at the point of inversion.

Let $F$ be a field, let $n\ge 1$, and let $b\in F^n$.

1. If $L\in M_n(F)$ is lower triangular with nonzero diagonal, the forward
   substitution recursion of
   [[def-forward-and-back-substitution-for-triangular-systems]] produces the
   unique solution of $Lx=b$.
2. If $U\in M_n(F)$ is upper triangular with nonzero diagonal, the backward
   substitution recursion produces the unique solution of $Ux=b$.

Each solve uses exactly $n$ divisions,
$\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ multiplications, and $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ additions or
subtractions, hence $O(n^2)$ scalar operations.

derivations.claim: The Euclidean state and observation spaces are standard Borel. By [F1], the finite path model uses Gaussian laws with the declared positive-semidefinite covariances; [F2] identifies its path law as jointly Gaussian, including when singular. The general existence result [F4] supplies the conditional-law setting, and [F3] fixes the initial filtering kernel as $\pi_0(*)=N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$ on the singleton empty history. This is a probability by [F9] and [F12], and is an RCD of $X_0$ given the trivial history because its event integral is exactly the $X_0$ marginal. The initial covariance is positive semidefinite by hypothesis. At every later step the algorithm is defined on its stated domain: $S_k\succ0$ has the Cholesky factor required by [F8].

Fix $k\in\{1,\ldots,T\}$ and assume inductively that the algorithm's $\pi_{k-1}$ is a filtering kernel with deterministic covariance $P_{k-1|k-1}\succeq0$. The vectors $X_{k-1}$ and $Y_{1:k-1}$ are measurable functions of $X_0,q_1,r_1,\ldots,q_{k-1},r_{k-1}$; by [F1,F13], the new pair $(q_k,r_k)$ is independent of that past. Apply [F5] with this past conditional law and push forward by $(x,q,r)\mapsto(F_kx+q,H_k(F_kx+q)+r)$. For each history $h$, the resulting conditional law of $(X_k,Y_k)$ is the one-step Gaussian block in [F6] with $m=m_{k-1|k-1}(h)$ and $P=P_{k-1|k-1}$. Its predicted covariance is positive semidefinite because $u^TP_{k|k-1}u=(F_k^Tu)^TP_{k-1|k-1}(F_k^Tu)+u^TQ_ku\ge0$. The positive-definite condition on $S_k$ allows [F7] to condition this block, for every $y_k$, with mean $m_{k|k-1}+P_{k|k-1}H_k^TS_k^{-1}v_k$ and covariance $P_{k|k-1}-P_{k|k-1}H_k^TS_k^{-1}H_kP_{k|k-1}$, exactly the algorithm's gain and update. The covariance is positive semidefinite by [F7]. To identify the computed gain, put $B_k=H_kP_{k|k-1}$. The algorithm's two triangular solves, applied columnwise, give $L_kU_k=B_k$ and $L_k^TK_k^T=U_k$. The diagonal entries of $L_k$ and $L_k^T$ are positive, so [F14] gives the unique solution of each column system. Therefore $S_kK_k^T=L_k(L_k^TK_k^T)=L_kU_k=B_k$; since $S_k\succ0$, this yields $K_k^T=S_k^{-1}B_k$, the gain in [F6]. The updated mean is affine in $(h,y_k)$ and the covariance is deterministic, so [F10] makes the Gaussian sections a measurable probability kernel.

Let $J_k(h,\cdot)$ be the conditional law of $(X_k,Y_k)$ given the previous history constructed in step 2.1, and let $M_k(h,\cdot)$ be its observation marginal. The one-step conditional identity [F7] gives $J_k(h,A\times B)=\int_B\pi_k(h,y_k,A)\,M_k(h,dy_k)$ for Borel state $A$ and observation set $B$. Integrating this identity over any Borel set $D$ of previous histories yields $\mathbb P(X_k\in A,Y_{1:k-1}\in D,Y_k\in B)=\int_D\int_B\pi_k(h,y_k,A)\,M_k(h,dy_k)\,\mathbb P_{Y_{1:k-1}}(dh)$. Since $M_k$ is the observation marginal of $J_k$, the iterated kernel is the joint law of $(Y_{1:k-1},Y_k)$ integrated against $\pi_k$. Thus this is the RCD identity on every rectangle $D\times B$; these rectangles form a pi-system generating the product history sigma-algebra, so [F11] extends the identity to all Borel history events. Therefore $\pi_k$ is a filtering kernel by [F3].

The base case is step 1.1, and steps 2.1–3.1 establish the induction step for every $k$, preserving positive semidefiniteness of the updated covariance. For $T=0$ only the base case applies. Hence the stated recursions give a conditional-law version at every history, with no inversion except of positive-definite innovation matrices. Different RCD versions may still differ on observation histories of probability zero.

Steps 1.1–2.1 allow PSD singular state and noise covariances while requiring only S_k to be SPD.
Step 1.1 handles the empty-history initial filter, and step 4.1 states the T=0 case.

risk_review.notes: Read all four proof steps and every current direct cited supplier, including the full batch-41 existence theorem and published finite Gaussian path proof. Positive Euclidean dimensions and AC match the model, Gaussian and conditioning suppliers. Base case is the constant initial probability on the empty-history singleton, also covering T=0. At each step, finite mutual noise independence implies independence of (q_k,r_k) from (X_{k-1},past observations); the reviewed noise-extension lemma then constructs the correct pointwise Gaussian block for every history. Covariance is deterministic and stays PSD, S_k alone is SPD, and two columnwise triangular solves yield S_k K_k^T = H_k Pminus. For each state event, conditional identities first hold on past/current observation rectangles; extending the conditional-law identity to bounded measurable functions by simple approximation identifies the iterated observation kernel with the actual history law. Both directions of the covariance-form equivalence follow from equality, and no converse model or stability claim is made. Reader and refuter report no finding; independent review finds none.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Fix a finite-horizon model from
[[def-linear-gaussian-state-space-model-with-independent-noises]] with
state and observation equations
$$X_k=F_kX_{k-1}+q_k,\qquad Y_k=H_kX_k+r_k\qquad (1\le k\le T),$$
where $X_0\sim N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$, the centered Gaussian noises $q_k,r_k$ are
mutually independent across times and from $X_0$, and $P_0,Q_k,R_k$ are
symmetric positive semidefinite. Let the parameters and observations be
admissible for [[alg-kalman-filter]], so the recursively formed innovation
covariances
$$S_k=H_kP_{k|k-1}H_k^T+R_k$$
are positive definite for every $1\le k\le T$. Run that algorithm from
$m_{0|0}=m_0$ and $P_{0|0}=P_0$. Then, for each $0\le k\le T$, the map
$$\pi_k(y_{1:k},\cdot)=N_{d_k}(m_{k|k}(y_{1:k}),P_{k|k})$$
is an everywhere-defined filtering kernel for $X_k$ given $Y_{1:k}$ in the
sense of [[def-state-space-filtering-laws]]. The empty history at $k=0$ is a
singleton, and $\pi_0=N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$. In particular, these recursions
give an exact Gaussian conditional-law version at every observation history;
each $P_{k|k}$ is positive semidefinite. Singular initial, process,
measurement, predicted-state, and filtered-state covariances are allowed.
Equivalently, the covariance update can be written in Joseph form
$$P_{k|k}=(I-K_kH_k)P_{k|k-1}(I-K_kH_k)^T+K_kR_kK_k^T.$$
Only the innovation matrices being solved must be positive definite. No
pointwise uniqueness of a conditional-law version on null histories,
observation-density assumption, or numerical-stability claim is made.

derivations.claim: Set $m_{0|0}=0$, $P_{0|0}=1$, $F_1=H_1=1$, and $Q_1=R_1=1$. The covariances are positive semidefinite and the noises satisfy [F2]. The prediction is $m_{1|0}=0$ and $P_{1|0}=1\cdot1\cdot1+1=2$. Thus $S_1=1\cdot2\cdot1+1=3>0$, and for $y_1=2$ the innovation is $v_1=2$.

Solving the scalar innovation system gives $K_1=2/3$. Therefore $m_{1|1}=0+(2/3)2=4/3$ and $P_{1|1}=2-(2/3)3(2/3)=2/3$. By [F1], the selected conditional-law version at $y_1=2$ is exactly $N(4/3,2/3)$.

Step 2.1 gives a normalized Gaussian filtering-kernel section.

finite_checks.claim: For prior N(0,1), Q=R=1, H=F=1, and y1=2, S1=3 and the exact filter is N(4/3,2/3).

derivations.claim: The matrix $P_{0|0}$ is positive semidefinite because $u^TP_{0|0}u=(u_1+u_2)^2\ge0$; it is singular because $P_{0|0}(1,-1)^T=0$. Since $\mathbb E Z=0$ and $\operatorname{Var}(Z)=1$, the Gaussian realization $X_0=(Z,Z)^T$ has covariance $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}=P_{0|0}$. With $Q_1=0$ and $F_1=I_2$, prediction gives $m_{1|0}=(0,0)^T$ and $P_{1|0}=P_{0|0}$.

Since $H_1=(1\ \ 0)$ and $R_1=1$, $S_1=H_1P_{1|0}H_1^T+R_1=2>0$. Hence $K_1=P_{1|0}H_1^TS_1^{-1}=(1/2,1/2)^T$ and $m_{1|1}=(1,1)^T$. The covariance update is $P_{1|1}=P_{1|0}-K_1S_1K_1^T=\begin{pmatrix}1/2&1/2\\1/2&1/2\end{pmatrix}$, which is still singular and positive semidefinite. By [F1] this is the exact filtering-kernel covariance at $y_1=2$, despite the singular prior covariance.
